question: Over three weeks a team refined the instructions for a Claude-drafted internal newsletter until the editor was consistently happy with every draft. Nobody asked the readers. What is the greatest risk?
options: A) The three weeks of refinement consumed effort that could have gone into writing newsletters.
B) The instructions have grown long enough that new team members will find them hard to follow at first.
C) The drafts are now tuned to one editor's taste, and no one has checked that they serve the readers.
D) The editor may become the only person able to judge whether a draft is ready to be published.
correct_answers: C) The drafts are now tuned to one editor's taste, and no one has checked that they serve the readers.
explanations: The refinement effort is a sunk cost that will be repaid if the arrangement works. Time spent iterating is expected; the problem is what the iteration was aimed at.
Long instructions are an onboarding inconvenience that can be tidied up. They make the arrangement harder to hand over, but they do not make the newsletter less effective for the people reading it.

Correct. Iteration improves whatever it is measured against, and here the only measure was one editor's approval. Three weeks of refinement have optimised for a proxy, so the drafts could satisfy the editor completely while serving readers worse than before.

Concentrating judgment in one person is a genuine weakness in the design, and it follows from the same root cause. It is a consequence of tuning to one taste rather than the primary danger, which is that readers were never consulted.
